In characterizing sleep and circadian health, the day�to�day regularity of sleep-wake timing 34 strongly predicts health outcomes, outperforming short sleep duration in prospective associations 35 with mortality and new-onset disease (1, 2). It is unknown whether biological (e.g., sleep and 36 circadian physiology) and sociocultural (e.g., exposures that affect sleep-wake timing) sex 37 differences lead to differences in day�to�day sleep-wake regularity or modify its prospective 38 associations with health outcomes. Here, we present findings from a UK Biobank study of 39 506,582 person-days of accelerometer recordings across 73,647 middle-aged adults preceding 40 549,009 person-years of follow-up. We compared SRI scores between males and females and 41 evaluated whether all�cause, cardiovascular, and cancer mortality differed across SRI groups by 42 sex. Custom contrasts were used to compare estimated marginal means across specific SRI-sex 43 combinations. Females were overrepresented among very high (SRI ≥90) and underrepresented 44 among very low (SRI <60) groups. After adjustment for demographic, health, and behavioral 45 covariates, males still had higher odds than females of exhibiting SRI <60. Low SRI and male sex 46 were synergistically associated with higher mortality rate. Demographic, health, and behavioral 47 covariate-adjusted models showed stronger and more dose�dependent associations between 48 low SRI and mortality among males than females. Although the omnibus SRI × sex interaction 49 terms were not statistically significant, the interaction contrast for SRI <60 versus ≥90 differed by 50 sex, suggesting a possible sex difference in mortality rates at very low SRI. Together, our findings 51 suggest that males may be more vulnerable than females to the mortality risk associated with 52 highly irregular sleep-wake schedules. 53

Main Text 54 55 Introduction 56 57 Conceptualization of sleep health has evolved from a focus on the absence of diagnosable 58 disorders to a multidimensional construct, with core components of duration, satisfaction, daytime 59 alertness, efficiency, timing, and regularity (3–7). Sleep regularity has garnered increased 60 attention as measures of intraindividual variability in dimensions of sleep health, rather than mean 61 measures alone, have demonstrated distinct health implications, a point reinforced by a 2024 62 National Sleep Foundation sleep timing and variability panel, which concluded that sleep 63 regularity is important for health, safety, and performance (8, 9). 64 65 Traditional metrics of sleep regularity (e.g., standard deviations of bedtime, wake time, or 66 duration) are constrained by their reliance on multi-day averages or conventional dispersion 67 measures and by the implicit assumption of a single main sleep episode (10). These limitations 68 are particularly pronounced when characterizing sleep regularity among individuals with multiple 69 daily sleep episodes (e.g., primary nocturnal sleep plus daytime naps), irregular work hours (e.g., 70 shift work), abrupt phase shifts (e.g., social or travel-associated jet lag (11)) unconventional 71 cycles (e.g., polyphasic sleep (8)), which contribute to circadian disruption that is not necessarily 72 reflected in measures such as the standard deviation of nocturnal sleep duration. Incidentally, 73 these scenarios are prevalent due to modern social and occupational demands (12), shift work 74 (13), and widespread evening use of light�emitting devices (14), all of which can contribute to 75 irregular daily schedules with misalignment between internal biological time and external 76 demands. 77 78 These limitations were addressed with the development of the Sleep Regularity Index (SRI) (10, 79 15), which quantifies the probability of being in the same state (asleep or awake) at the same 80 clock time on consecutive days, capturing day-to-day sleep regularity accommodating multiple 81 sleep bouts and sudden schedule changes across the 24�hour cycle. High day-to-day variability 82 in sleep-wake timing as measured by the SRI is prospectively associated with higher rates of all- 83 cause mortality and cause-specific mortality due to cardiometabolic disease and cancer (1, 16, 84 17). These relationships, which appear robust to adjustment for sleep duration and are observed 85 across multiple antecedent risk states (9, 18–23), are hypothesized to reflect a combination of 86 harmful effects of recurrent inconsistencies in the patterns of environmental exposures (e.g., light- 87 dark cycles (15, 24, 25)), behaviors (e.g., sleep-wake, feeding-fasting cycles), and circadian 88 rhythms (i.e., endogenous time-varying physiology (10, 15)). Laboratory and epidemiological 89 evidence indicate that repeated circadian misalignment and irregular exposure to circadian 90 synchronizers may, in turn, adversely affect glucose metabolism, blood pressure regulation, 91 autonomic balance, inflammation, and hormonal rhythms, thereby increasing long-term risk for a 92 range of adverse health conditions across organ systems and pathogenic pathways (9, 26–31). In 93 2023, Feng et al. reported that among 16 accelerometer-measured rest-activity parameters, lower 94 relative amplitude of rest-activity rhythms showed the strongest or second-strongest prospective 95 associations with 9 new-onset chronic health conditions (32). More recently, a Phenome-Wide 96 Association Study (PheWAS) comparing SRI and short sleep duration found that SRI predicted 97 risk for more than twice as many diseases (131 versus 63, respectively), and that sleep regularity 98 was a significantly stronger predictor for ten times as many outcomes (90 versus 9, respectively) 99 (2). 100 101 Sex differences in circadian biology are well-characterized and exist at multiple levels, from 102 anatomy to physiology and behavior and to responses to perturbations (33–35). Laboratory 103 studies demonstrate that males exhibit longer average intrinsic circadian periods than females 104 (36), that sleep initiation in males tends to occur at an earlier circadian phase relative to dim light 105 melatonin onset (37), and that sex modulates the effects of circadian misalignment on energy 106 metabolism (38). The authors also describe enhanced entrainment to 112 phase shifts and more resilience to genetic and environmental circadian disruption among 113 females than males and propose adaptation to frequent nocturnal awakenings associated with 114 caring for offspring as an underlying selective evolutionary pressure. 115 116 Relatedly, multiple dimensions of sleep health feature sex differences (41), including in sleep 117 homeostasis in response to sleep deprivation (42), as well as in the prevalence and presentation 118 of sleep disorders such as insomnia (~1.4:1 female:male ratio (43)) and sleep-disordered 119 breathing (e.g., obstructive sleep apnea, 3:1 to 5:1 male:female ratio, with distinct female disease 120 phenotypes (44)). Emerging evidence suggests that the higher rates of new�onset heart rhythm 121 disorders (e.g., cardiac arrhythmias, conduction disorders) observed at lower SRI scores are 122 primarily driven by stronger associations in males than females (45, 46). Yet sex differences in 123 the SRI have not yet been rigorously investigated. Analyses of two independent cohorts have 124 reported that female individuals achieved moderately higher SRI scores than did males (e.g., UK 125 Biobank adults [females mean SRI +1.2] (47); NHANES adults [females median SRI +2.4] (48)). 126 However, the distribution of SRI scores by sex remains unknown, and the interaction between 127 sex, sleep-wake regularity, and mortality is similarly under-studied. The presence of sex 128 differences in associations between SRI and mortality warrants examination, as differences would 129 raise the possibility of sex-divergent pathophysiologic mechanisms that accentuate or attenuate 130 SRI-related risk relationships. 131 132 To begin to address these questions, we used data from a prospective cohort of middle-aged 133 adult participants in the UK Biobank (49) to perform a study in three parts. Discussion 275 276 In this study of 506,582 person-days of accelerometer-derived sleep-wake data collected from 277 73,647 middle-aged adults (female n = 41,489 [56.3%]), despite numerically similar median 278 scores, females exhibited a more favorable distribution of day�to�day sleep-wake timing than did 279 males, with greater representation in the highest SRI group and lower representation in the 280 lowest group. Over a median 7.5-year follow-up interval, consistent with recent literature (1, 16), 281 less regular day�to�day sleep-wake timing was associated with higher all-cause and cause- 282 specific mortality rates; however, we report for the first time that these associations differed both 283 between and within sexes. Between�sex comparisons revealed that among the least regular 284 sleepers, all-cause mortality risk was approximately twice as high in males as in females, 285 whereas risk did not differ between sexes among the most regular sleepers. Within�sex 286 comparisons showed stronger SRI-mortality associations in males than females, with significance 287 persisting after adjustment for demographics, baseline health, and health behaviors (i.e., 288 smoking, alcohol, physical activity, sleep duration) among males (e.g., all-cause mortality aHR = 289 1.8 [1.2–2.5]; p <0.001) but not females. These sex-specific dose-dependent SRI-mortality 290 associations suggest that males may have excess vulnerability to highly irregular sleep�wake 291 cycles and their environmental and circadian correlates beyond mechanisms shared by both 292 sexes. 293 294 Our findings reveal that on average, males both exhibit more extreme irregularity in day�to�day 295 sleep-wake timing and experience heightened mortality risks at high levels of irregularity, 296 resulting in the steeper observed SRI-mortality relationships. The potential mechanisms 297 underlying these hypothesis-generating findings warrant investigation. Sex differences in 298 environmental, occupational, and social exposures; clustering of health behaviors, circadian 299 biology, and sleep physiology; and cardiometabolic and inflammatory responses may together 300 shape exposure to and consequences of highly irregular sleep-wake patterns. For example, 301 highly irregular versus regular day-to-day sleep-wake timing is associated with later dim-light 302 melatonin onset and lower amplitude light-dark exposure rhythms (15, 25). With light-dark cycles 303 serving as the principal circadian synchronizer in mammals (51, 52), circadian dysregulation has 304 been proposed to account for why suboptimal light exposure profiles (53) have been associated 305 with higher prospective rates of mood disorders (54), cardiometabolic disease (55–58), and 306 mortality (24). 307 308 Between�sex comparisons showed that the higher male mortality risk was attenuated by high 309 sleep regularity. Males in the least regular SRI group exhibited twice the all-cause mortality rate 310 of similarly irregular females, whereas mortality rates were not significantly different by sex in the 311 most regular SRI group, suggesting that higher sleep regularity may protect against excess male 312 mortality risk. Attenuation of excess male mortality among the most regular sleepers was 313 particularly evident for cardiovascular mortality. Through early September 2025, ischemic heart 314 disease was the leading cause of male death in the UK Biobank, with more than twice as many 315 deaths as those attributable to the second�leading cause (59). In contrast, ischemic heart 316 disease ranked fourth among females, trailing two cancers (lung, breast) and dementia. Irregular 317 sleep confers greater cardiometabolic risk through chronic circadian misalignment (26, 60), 318 autonomic nervous system imbalances with sympathetic overactivation (26), impaired nocturnal 319 blood pressure dipping (61, 62), and adverse metabolic and inflammatory profiles (38, 63), all of 320 which contribute to atherosclerosis, arrhythmogenesis, and ultimately ischemic heart disease 321 (64). 322 323 Given higher baseline cardiometabolic morbidity and less favorable autonomic and vascular 324 aging trajectories among males than among females (65), more regular sleep-wake timing may 325 stabilize these pathways in males, disproportionately reducing their risk of ischemic heart disease 326 and narrowing the male-female cardiovascular mortality disparity that is otherwise observed in the 327 UK Biobank. In 364 contrast, they persisted in males, suggesting residual SRI�associated risk among males. 365 Whether the residual risk relates to sex�specific biological (e.g., heightened vulnerability to 366 sleep- and circadian-related autonomic and cardiometabolic dysregulation) or behavioral 367 vulnerabilities (e.g., unmeasured health behaviors, male�dominated occupational schedules, 368 environmental and time-of-day varying exposures) to irregular sleep-wake cycles warrants 369 investigation, especially given that male sex and low SRI conferred additive mortality risks, such 370 that males in the least regular SRI group had 140% (fully adjusted) to 300% (minimally adjusted) 371 higher risk of all-cause mortality than females in the most regular SRI group. In contrast, all-cause 372 mortality risk did not differ between males in the most regular SRI group and females in the least 373 regular SRI group (aHRs = 0.74 to 1.15, ps = 0.34 to 0.97). 374 375 While the persistence of SRI�associated risk among males after multivariable adjustment merits 376 attention, attenuation of SRI-mortality associations in both sexes with adjustment for 377 demographic, health, and behavioral factors also identifies potential avenues for risk modification. 378 The contributions of baseline cardiometabolic status, mental health, smoking, alcohol use, 379 physical inactivity, and other modifiable behaviors suggest that individuals with irregular sleep 380 may derive benefit from interventions targeting characteristics that co-occur with irregular sleep, 381 especially while the degree to which the day-to-day regularity of sleep-wake timing is modifiable 382 remains uncertain. 383 384

Our identification of a sex difference in the relationship between the day-to-day regularity of 385 sleep-wake timing and mortality extends a rapidly expanding literature (50), which has thus far 386 largely examined associations between SRI and health or performance at the population or 387 sample level rather than characterizing how these relationships differ within population 388 subgroups. Three recent studies (one peer-reviewed) have reported sex differences in 389 associations between low SRI and health outcomes (2, 45, 48). The peer-reviewed study, 390 published in 2026, found that among 7,085 US adults in the National Health and Nutrition 391 Examination Survey, the highest versus lowest SRI quintile was associated with 8% lower BMI, 392 with a stronger relationship among females (48). In a 2025 conference abstract, among UK 393 Biobank participants (n = 69,725), lower SRI scores were reported to be associated with a higher 394 rate of new-onset heart rhythm disorders (e.g., cardiac arrhythmias and conduction disorders), a 395 relationship that was most pronounced among male participants and especially those with 396 baseline cardiovascular disease (45). A 2026 preprint reported a PheWAS with the SRI among 397 UK Biobank participants (n = 60,998), identifying that 131 of 199 (65.8%) conditions were 398 predicted by SRI (2). Both studies found sex-specific risk elevation of similar magnitude for 399 cardiac dysrhythmias among males as compared to females (2, 45). 400 401 Interestingly, the PheWAS study of new�onset conditions diagnosed one or more years after 402 accelerometer recording found that circulatory disorders were among those most consistently 403 linked with irregular sleep among females but not males (2).
